title: Diageo targets US$1bn in savings as Dave Lewis unveils turnaround plan
summary:
Diageo has launched a three-year programme to improve efficiency and restore growth under new chief executive Sir Dave Lewis. The drinks group will target an additional US$1 billion in cost savings while ruling out further acquisitions or major asset disposals.

The post Diageo targets US$1bn in savings as Dave Lewis unveils turnaround plan appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Diageo has launched a three-year programme to improve efficiency and restore growth under new chief executive Sir Dave Lewis. The drinks group will target an additional US$1 billion in cost savings while ruling out further acquisitions or major asset disposals. After six months reviewing Diageo, new chief executive Sir Dave Lewis has launched a programme to reinvigorate the world's largest premium spirits group. Significantly, he said he does not intend to pursue any further mergers or acquisitions, or dispose of additional assets once the sales of East African Breweries and the Royal Challengers Bangalore cricket franchise have been completed. Lewis intends to strip an additional US$1 billion in costs from the business over the next three years, over and above the existing US$650 million programme, which is largely complete. He plans to achieve this by redesigning the operating model and overhauling the supply chain. He refused to be drawn on the number of job cuts involved but pointed out that there are many inefficiencies created by duplication across the company. Diageo has budgeted for US$514 million in severance costs.

Investing through cost savings

In the coming year, Diageo expects organic sales to remain broadly flat and operating profit to grow by a low to mid-single-digit percentage, supported by cost savings. “The savings will allow us to invest in innovation selectively where we need to improve our competitiveness, but they also allow us to do so without needing to reduce operating profit,” Lewis said. A key focus will be ready-to-drink products, where Lewis has said the group is underperforming. The announcement prompted a 6.5% rise in Diageo's share price, which was also supported by a moderate improvement in the company's results for the year to the end of June.

Results edge ahead of expectations

Diageo's net sales fell by 3% to US$19.6 billion, while organic sales declined by 2%. However, the group's operating profit increased by 2%. Reported group operating profit fell 27% to US$3.2 billion, reflecting US$900 million of restructuring charges and a US$1.5 billion impairment, largely related to the impact of hyperinflationary accounting and pricing changes in Turkey. The results were slightly ahead of analysts' forecasts.

China and North America remain difficult

The biggest headwinds in the latest results came from Chinese baijiu and the North American market. Without the effects of Beijing's policies on baijiu, organic net sales would have been only half a percentage point lower than in 2025 and organic operating profit would have increased by 4.5%. Although the company reported growth in Europe, Latin America and Africa, chief financial officer Nik Jhangiani said the "biggest challenge" remained North America, where organic sales fell by 8.4% as tequila sales dropped by 21%.

Outlook for the year ahead

Diageo expects to gain market share in North America next year but warned that sales in the region would decline by a mid-single-digit percentage. Lewis said there was "hard work ahead" before the company returned to growth in the market in around two years. For the coming financial year, Diageo expects organic sales to remain broadly flat and operating profit to grow by a low to mid-single-digit percentage, supported by the planned cost savings.

title: Harvest 2026: Sicily’s 100-day odyssey begins
summary:
Sicily is picking its 2026 harvest under kinder skies, two vintages after a drought that brought the island to its knees. It is also, this summer, the most photographed coastline on earth. The trade should notice that these two facts belong in the same sentence, writes Filippo Bartolotta.

The post Harvest 2026: Sicily’s 100-day odyssey begins appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Sicily is picking its 2026 harvest under kinder skies, two vintages after a drought that brought the island to its knees. It is also, this summer, the most photographed coastline on earth. The trade should notice that these two facts belong in the same sentence, writes Filippo Bartolotta.

The 2026 Sicilian harvest started this week in the west, with the first early-ripening white varieties coming off the vine. From here it will run for roughly a hundred days – across the western coast, into the interior, up onto the Iblean plateau, round to the Strait of Messina, out to the smaller islands, and finally to Etna, where picking may not finish until the first days of November. No other European wine region asks its growers to work a calendar that long. Sicily is not a region. It is a continent that happens to be an island, packed with more than 70 indigenous varieties and an extraordinary climatic and geological diversity. This year, the news is good. And that, oddly, is what makes the story worth telling.

Remember 2024

Two harvests ago, Sicily was on its knees. The island endured its worst drought in nearly two decades. Rome declared a state of emergency in early May 2024, water was rationed across more than ninety municipalities, and the farmers’ association Coldiretti put agricultural damage at €2.7 billion in the first seven months of the year alone, with the wheat harvest collapsing by more than half. Researchers at World Weather Attribution concluded that climate change was a key driver. Growers picked up to ten days early, not because the fruit was ready but because there was nothing left to wait for. It is worth adding the part that rarely makes the international press: Sicily’s water network leaks more than half of what enters it. ISTAT put network losses at almost 52% in 2022. The drought was meteorological. The crisis was also administrative. Against that backdrop, 2026 reads like a reprieve. In its 2026 harvest report, the producers’ association Assovini Sicilia strikes an unmistakably relieved tone. "A particularly rainy winter and spring allowed a good restoration of soil water reserves," says vice-president Pietro Pollara. Continuing, he says, "Even July’s temperature peaks were well managed by the plants thanks to the accumulated water availability," adding, "We expect a high-quality harvest, with wines showing an interesting aromatic profile and good balance between freshness and elegance." A wet winter is welcome, but it is not a long-term strategy.

An overlooked strength

Here is where Sicily has something the rest of the wine world is quietly starting to want. Most Sicilian viticulture is dry-farmed. Not as a lifestyle choice, not as a marketing badge, but because for centuries there was no alternative. The result is a body of practical knowledge about growing vines without water that Bordeaux, Napa and the Languedoc are now paying consultants to reconstruct from scratch. The clearest expression of it sits on Pantelleria, where the vite ad alberello (head-trained bush vine) was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in November 2014. It was the first agricultural practice ever to receive the honour. The technique is deceptively simple: vines are planted in hollows dug some 20cm into the ground. The depression shelters the plant from a wind that never stops, retains soil moisture, and catches what little rain falls. Around 5,000 islanders farm a plot this way. That is not folklore. That is a functioning water-management system with no moving parts and no energy cost. The same logic operates at Noto. "Extreme heat is faced thanks to the skilful alberello cultivation of the vines," says Gionata Pulignami, technical director at Zisola. "The absence of a structure allows free circulation of the cooler currents and the sea breezes." A trellis catches heat and blocks air. A bush vine does neither.

Homer got there first

Perhaps the most remarkable connection is that it was described almost 2,700 years ago by Homer. In Book IX of the Odyssey, Odysseus describes the land of the Cyclopes. They neither plant nor plough, he reports; wheat, barley and vines heavy with grapes come up unsown and untilled, and the rain of Zeus alone brings them on. Strip away the hexameter and that is a technical description of rain-fed, unirrigated Mediterranean agriculture. It is arguably the oldest written account of dry farming we have – and Greek tradition has always placed the Cyclopes in Sicily, at the foot of Etna, where the Faraglioni dei Ciclopi still stand off Aci Trezza as the rocks Polyphemus threw. Homer also gives us wine’s first recorded weaponisation. Odysseus escapes the cave because he has brought a wine so concentrated it was normally cut twenty parts water to one, and the Cyclops drinks it neat. High alcohol, low dilution, catastrophic consequences: the Sicilian wine industry spent the late twentieth century living out that same story in bulk tankers. It has spent the last twenty-five years getting out of it. The oldest written description of dry farming may be a Greek poem about a Sicilian hillside. The oldest written cautionary tale about alcohol is on the next page. This matters commercially right now for one reason. Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey opened on 16 July 2026 to what box-office trade reporting has called the biggest global opening of his career. It was shot on location over 91 days on 70mm IMAX, and its principal Italian set was Favignana, in the Egadi islands off Trapani, with the Castello di Santa Caterina crowning Monte Santa Caterina among the key locations. The Aeolian islands feature too. Travel platforms are already reporting a surge in set-jetting searches. Look at where that camera was pointing. Favignana sits twenty minutes by hydrofoil from Trapani and Marsala – the exact corner of western Sicily where this harvest began last week, where Grillo grows, where Marsala was invented by English merchants in the 1770s. The Aeolians are Salina, and Salina is Malvasia. "The forecasts at Salina are positive and exciting," says Pietro Colosi, oenologist at the Colosi winery, "the result of a season that found a perfect balance for all the typical varieties of this territory, starting with Malvasia, which will deliver a very high qualitative standard, and wines of remarkable aromatic complexity and freshness." A sweet, saline, sun-dried wine from a volcanic island in the middle of an IMAX blockbuster about a sailor trying to get home. That is not a wine list entry. That is a scene.

A timely opportunity

Set-jetting has a short half-life. The film is in cinemas now, the harvest runs to November, and the two calendars overlap almost exactly – 91 days of shooting, a hundred days of picking. Sicily has perhaps one trading quarter in which the world’s most valuable free advertising campaign is running on its behalf. What the trade could do with it, concretely: a by-the-glass "Odyssey" flight of western Sicilian whites and Aeolian Malvasia; Egadi and Aeolian cellar doors packaging tastings against the ferry timetable rather than the tour-bus one; importers pulling Salina and Trapani listings forward rather than waiting for the spring campaign; sommeliers given one usable line – that Homer described these vineyards before anyone thought to name them. Producers on Favignana and the Egadi should be talking to location-tourism operators this month, not next spring. The risk is the obvious one. Cinematic borrowed interest sells a first bottle; it does not sell a second. Which brings us back to what is actually in the glass.

Variety as adaptation

The second Sicilian asset is genetic. Grillo – itself a 19th-century Sicilian crossing – has become the island’s proof of concept. "Western Sicily gives us Grillo as a resilient variety, capable of facing difficult climatic conditions," says Giampiero Vantaggiato, agronomist at Feudo Stagnone & Cantine Birgi, who also reports excellent vegetative behaviour from Nero d’Avola and Perricone. In the Ragusa hills, Frappato is doing something more interesting than merely surviving. "Vigorous and resistant to the scorching heat," say Carlo Casavecchia and Gaetana Jacono of Valle dell’Acate, the grapes point to "a complex Frappato, an unusual red, elegant and in step with the times." Light, fresh, chillable Mediterranean reds are precisely the category the trade is short of. On Pantelleria, warming has cut both ways. Zibibbo’s performance "has not been called into question by rising temperatures," reports Gianfranco Giacalone of Cantine Pellegrino – instead it has produced "a particularly balanced sugar-acid ratio," with a staggered harvest from coastal contrade up to the late mountain plots. And on Etna, altitude does the work that irrigation does elsewhere. Salvatore Rizzuto, oenologist at Gambino, points to the volcano’s continental climate delivering healthy Nerello Mascalese and Carricante with "an interesting balance between phenolic maturity and acidity." Polyphemus, one notes, would have been drinking from these slopes.

A note of caution

Not everyone is relaxed. In the Mamertino DOC, Antonio Grasso of Feudo Solaria is deliberately withholding judgement: "We are cautious. It will be important to understand how Nocera reacts, a variety particularly sensitive to high temperatures." That single sentence is the most valuable line in the entire harvest report. Sicily’s adaptive toolkit is real, but it is not universal, and the varieties that struggle will struggle regardless of how good the winter rain was. There is a commercial fragility too. Alberello is hand-worked, low-yielding and expensive. It survives on Pantelleria because 5,000 people are stubborn about it. Scale that economics across a warming Mediterranean and the maths gets uncomfortable fast. The key point for the trade is this. Sicily spent two centuries learning to farm without water because it had to. The rest of the wine world is about to need that curriculum. Odysseus took ten years to get home and the story is still earning. Sicily has a hundred days and a camera crew’s worth of goodwill. The question is whether the island gets paid for the knowledge – or simply watches everyone else patent it.

title: Jeremy Clarkson launches beer and beef pies
summary:
Jeremy Clarkson’s beer and beef pies are hitting pub menus this month. db finds out more about what they contain and where you can try them.

The post Jeremy Clarkson launches beer and beef pies appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Jeremy Clarkson’s beer and beef pies are hitting pub menus this month. db finds out more about what they contain and where you can try them. The pies, which will become available in 498 Marston’s pubs across the UK, have been made with Clarkson’s beer - specifically Hawkstone IPA - and also contain slow-cooked British beef in the filling.

Available for a limited-time

The beer and beef pie roll out is part of a limited-time specials offer and are set to boost sales across Marston’s pub menus and marks Hawkstone’s largest pub partnership to date. Describing the decision to team up with Clarkson's beer brand, Marston's director of brand activation Kiran Bains said: “We’re so excited to working with Hawkstone to bring our new take on a pub classic to almost 500 of our pubs across the UK. British beef and Hawkstone IPA are a match made in heaven, and we’ve created a really delicious dish to serve to guests up and down the country, introducing Hawkstone to more customers and giving them a new reason to visit their local. We can’t wait for everyone to try it.” Hawkstone sales director Andy Cross said: "The more Hawkstone you drink, the more barley we buy from British farmers. That’s why we’re thrilled Marston’s is serving Hawkstone IPA, not just by the bottle but also in a Great British pub classic, in almost 500 pubs nationwide.”

A way to 'celebrate the farming community'

Cross also advised beer and pie fans to “visit your local Marston’s pub" because that's where you can "tuck into a pie and help us celebrate the farming community before stocks run out". The complete description of the Hawkstone IPA and beef pie states that it features “British diced beef and pulled beef cheek, slow-cooked in a rich Hawkstone IPA gravy with seasonal vegetables and Barber’s Cheddar, all wrapped in buttery shortcrust pastry”. According to Marston’s, the pie will be “served with seasonal vegetables, extra gravy and a choice of chips or mash”. Plus, bottles of Hawkstone IPA will also be available at participating pubs so that the beer can be paired alongside any pie orders.

title: Quilceda Creek acquires full ownership of Champoux Vineyard
summary:
Washington winery Quilceda Creek, which has long owned a stake in the historic Champoux Vineyard, has now acquired the Horse Heaven Hills AVA site in full, saying it is a vineyard that "will go down in history".

The post Quilceda Creek acquires full ownership of Champoux Vineyard appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Washington winery Quilceda Creek, which has long owned a stake in the historic Champoux Vineyard, has now acquired the Horse Heaven Hills AVA site in full, saying it is a vineyard that "will go down in history". Quilceda Creek, which has been involved with Champoux Vineyard to various degrees for many decades, has snapped up the last remaining stake in the esteemed site, taking its interests from 79% to full ownership. The move is an important one for Quilceda Creek as it means it now has full control over the sourcing for its signature wine Columbia Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, which is made using grapes from Champoux. First planted in the early 1970s, Champoux was the first vineyard to be established in the Horse Heaven Hills AVA in Washington State's Columbia Valley. Considered by many to be the flagship and benchmark vineyard of the sub-region, it is known for its high-quality Cabernet Sauvignon grapes, and has provided fruit for Quilceda Creek's wines since 1986.

Upping the stakes

Quilceda Creek has gradually increased its ownership of the special site over the last 30 years, previously acquiring a 79% stake in August 2021. Comprising 153 acres (62ha) of vines, Champoux's quality "cannot be replicated" in any other location, according to Quilceda Creek's winemaker. "Champoux has noble tannins that creates a suave texture so unique to the site that it cannot be replicated,” said Paul Golitzin, Quilceda Creek's director of winemaking. “We are honoured and humbled to take care of this special piece of land.”

"Exceptional depth"

Such is Quilceda Creek's commitment to the vineyard that the producer has even helped to replant certain areas within it over the years, including after the site was struck by frost in 2010. Situated on south-facing slopes at 600-800 feet altitude, the vineyard is cooled by air flowing down from the surrounding higher elevations. These significant diurnal temperature shifts allow the fruit to ripen fully while preserving vibrant natural acidity, according to Quilceda Creek, "yielding balanced, age-worthy wines with exceptional depth and elegance." "Champoux is a vineyard that will go down in winegrowing history,” said vineyard manager Dan Nickolaus. “It’s an extraordinary site for red wine grapes, consistently producing fruit of the highest quality year after year." The Golitzen family, which owns Quilceda Creek, has been on an acquisition mission during the past 12 months, not only picking up Champoux but also a "pristine" vineyard planted with Bordeaux varieties on Red Mountain, Washington State’s smallest yet arguably most prestigious wine region, last September. The Golitzens subsequently renamed the site Ad Astra, and fruit from this location is also used in the producer's fine Cabernet Sauvignon-led wines. Columbia Valley is increasingly attracting interest from serious wine collectors across the globe, with CellarTracker founder Eric LeVine telling the drinks business that it is was the ninth “most purchased region” among Cellar Tracker users in 2025. That ranking places it ahead of the Rhône Valley, and not too far behind Champagne - the famous French sparkling region had 509,000 purchases on CellarTracker compared with Columbia Valley's 436,000.

title: ‘We’re still at experimentation level’: meet the Korean somm making wine for Hong Kong
summary:
Ever heard of Korean wine? No? Well, that's exactly what Ted Ko is trying to change. Under the Koyberpunk brand (a blend of terms "Korea" and "cyberpunk"), he produces a three-bottle bouquet of cabernet sauvignon, chardonnay-semillon blend and muscat bailey-A... but not for his home country. Joyce Yip reports.

The post ‘We’re still at experimentation level’: meet the Korean somm making wine for Hong Kong appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Ever heard of Korean wine? No? Well, that's exactly what Ted Ko is trying to change. Under the Koyberpunk brand (a blend of terms "Korea" and "cyberpunk"), he produces a three-bottle bouquet of cabernet sauvignon, chardonnay-semillon blend and muscat bailey-A... but not for his home country. Joyce Yip reports. When Ted Ko – Korea-born sommelier, wine merchant and writer – moved to Hong Kong in 2019, he was shocked at its wine drinkers’ curiosity for esoteric wine regions (think Croatia, Israel and India) yet disappointed at the subpar pairing options its restaurants had for Korean food.   “[Sommeliers] would pair Korean food with riesling, or wines from Torrontés, Argentina, bubbles or light pinot noir; but Korean food is umami and leans on a sweeter side. So, for me, those pairings don’t create a new flavour, only a complement at best,” he says.  So, in the same year, he made his own, interestingly, not for his home country. 

Why Ko mainly sells to Hong Kong

Named Koyberpunk – a portmanteau of “Korea” and “cyberpunk” – his portfolio of cabernet sauvignon, a chardonnay-semillon blend and muscat bailey-A is the fruit of a 1.5-acre vineyard in Yeongcheon-City, located 350km southeast of Seoul. Each varietal is aged for a year in a mix of American and Korean oak – which, according to Ko, is “neutral, similar to Italian oak”. Of his annual production of 8,000 bottles, however, only a small percentage is served at selected restaurants in the Korean capital. His cabernet sauvignon and chardonnay-semillon blend are exclusively available on-trade in Hong Kong, poured at the likes of his co-owned Korean restaurant O’RM, wine bar Brut and – when they fit its seasonal menu – at Michelin One-Starred Hansik Goo. For a price reference, both bottles are sold for HK$980 (£92.85) at Brut. The decision to pull muscat-bailey A from the Hong Kong market, Ko explains, is that sommeliers in the city’s high-end Korean restaurants “didn’t want a hybrid grape: they were worried about the brand positioning of the wine”. Ko is doubtful his wines would thrive in his home country, claiming that “unlike the patriotic Japanese and Mainland Chinese, most Koreans have a perception that good wines should come from Napa, Bordeaux and Burgundy… The general Korean wine consumer is not that mature yet,” he says. 

It's still early days for Korean wine

Since the early 2000s, the Korean government has offered subsidies to farmers willing to convert crops into secondary products – grains into flour, barley into beer and table grapes to wine. This resulted in an influx of aromatic and sweet wines with flavour profiles that are, according to Ko, akin to Moscato d’asti, befitting the country’s cuisine and its people’s sweet tooth.  “They are good grapes, but Korean farmers – most of them in their 60s and 70s – don’t really have the techniques to produce wines that can compete with the rest of the world,” he says. Unlike tipples in neighbouring Japan – which are demarked by a geographical indication– Ko says Korea-made wines are still at its nascency to “have a distinctive profile”.  “We’re still at an experimentation level,” he says. “Koyberpunk, for instance, tried to make cabernet franc but it just didn’t work. Korea is dotted with microclimates, so we don’t know what we’ll get until we try it out. We don’t have oenologists in the country.”

title: Chile’s 2026 harvest underlines regional identity
summary:
Chile’s harvest for 2026 is one that is “defined by precision, marked by technical consistency and with a clear regional identity across its leading valleys”, according to Viña Concha y Toro 2026 harvest report.

The post Chile’s 2026 harvest underlines regional identity appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: Chile’s harvest for 2026 is one that is “defined by precision, marked by technical consistency and with a clear regional identity across its leading valleys”, according to Viña Concha y Toro 2026 harvest report. The growing season varied from region to region, but benefitted from adequate rainfall in winter, which topped up the water levels, as well as a favourable spring that gave the vines a good start. The ripening period however “evolved at different paces  across coastal and inland regions”, CYT said, resulting in “a clear distinction between coastal influenced valleys and inland appellations… and distinctive final wine profiles.” In Limarí for example, there was above average rain during the winter, and the persistent morning cloud cover caused by the coastal fog (camanchaca) elevated the relative humidity and allowed a level of heat accumulation that favoured “slow, gradual and even ripening”, the company said, resulting in wines “with exceptional aromatic precision, marked tension and a distinct mineral profile”. This delayed start in Limarí contrasted to the more active start to the growing season in Maipo, Peumo and Maule however. Maipo, which is home to Viña Concha y Toro’s historic vineyards and the source of some of its finest Cabernet Sauvignons, benefitted from a good start in the spring, which was warmer than the previous year. This was followed by stable summer temperatures without extreme weather events, promoting “steady and uninterrupted ripening” that favoured concentrated fruit, “structural finesse and overall balance”. The weather in March and April was stable and dry, providing a broad harvest window, “allowing optimal picking decisions based on phenolic maturity”, it said. The resulting wine shows “remarkable structural coherence, with well-defined fruit, refined tannins and a depth and elegance fully consistent with the historical identity of the valley”, the company added. “The season unfolded under particularly favourable vineyard conditions, with adequate water availability, excellent fruit health and a growing cycle free from significant climatic disruptions,” it said. The weather in Peumo DO in the Cachapoal Valley (where the company’s Carmenere wines comes from), was particularly favourably for late-ripening varieties. Winter rains and an early start in the spring was checked by rainfall in March which helped cool things down at a critical stage. This moderated the pace of ripening and allowing a “gradual and uninterrupted evolution during a crucial period for achieving balance between technological and phenolic maturity”, the company said, resulting in wines with intensity, freshness, concentration and character. A similar rain event in the Maule required careful vineyard management and well-timed harvesting decisions, the company said. Merlot in San Clemente was predominantly harvested under ideal conditions before the rains, while in Cauquenes, performance was also highly positive, “producing wines with excellent fruit expression, softness and balance” it said. Reflecting on the harvest overall, Marcelo Papa, technical director of Viña Concha y Toro said the 2026 harvest “confirms that quality is built upon a precise understanding of each origin.” “Rather than being defined by extremes, it was a vintage in which balance and each vineyard’s ability to express its identity proved decisive”, he said. The company further noted that the 2026 harvest was "not defined by a single factor, but by the clarity with which each origin expressed its winemaking potential." "The coastal influence in Limarí, the structural stability of Maipo, the precise adjustment of the growing cycle in Peumo and the resilience demonstrated in Maule all contributed to a harvest of exceptional quality across the company’s portfolio, from Super Premium to Icon wines."

title: How Yunnan Red introduced a generation to locally-made wine
summary:
Second generation Yunnan Red proprietor Wynn Wu 0pens up about the ways one of the country’s oldest wineries is adapting to China’s evolving tastes. Rebecca Lo reports.

The post How Yunnan Red introduced a generation to locally-made wine appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Second generation Yunnan Red proprietor Wynn Wu 0pens up about the ways one of the country’s oldest wineries is adapting to China’s evolving tastes. Rebecca Lo reports. Wynn Wu recalled the first time he visited the vineyards of Yunnan Red. In 1997, his father Wu Kegang invested in the state-owned winery in Mile, approximately 150 kilometres south of the Yunnan provincial capital of Kunming.  Known for its abundant hours of sun, long growing season and high altitudes, Yunnan is ideal for winemaking. Yet 30 years ago, infrastructure was lacking.  “Getting there was a four hour drive from Kunming along a muddy road in pitch blackness – Yunnan was so rural at the time,” Wu grinned. “Now, Mile is a 35 minute ride on the high speed rail. The region has become a popular tourist destination.”  

Transforming the region

Mainland China was ripe for foreign investment in the 1990s. The Hong Kong-based Wu family knew that its US$10 million (£7.42 million) could make a big difference to the 20,000 farmers working the 1,600 hectares of vineyards in Dongfeng Farm. There was also a personal connection: Wu’s mother is from Yunnan.  The state-owned agricultural collective was already producing red and white wines from grapes planted by French missionaries in the 1860s. Wu Kegang expanded production to include grape juice, grappa and brandy alongside mass market and premium wines; today, its annual production totals up to four million bottles. Meanwhile, its skincare brand Namo contains grape seeds and skin extracts to reduce production waste. “My father saw that wine consumption was a growing sector for mainland China,” Wu noted. “His investment could help local farmers and invigorate the community.”   Today, the senior Wu remains very hands-on and continues to head the company while the junior Wu’s wife Phoenix Lee joined in 2019 to spearhead marketing efforts. 

All about the grapes

The grapes that make up Yunnan Red’s collection include Isabella, Baco Noir and Le Pourpre (Siebel 4646) grapes for reds, with the latter two French experimental varietals designed to resist phylloxera. Whites are primarily made from Niagara grapes. Due to the clay-rich terroir, 1,480 metre altitude and damp climate in Mile, experiments with varietals such as Chardonnay or Cabernet Sauvignon have been less successful than the ones already flourishing there.  “We make the most from what has proven to grow well,” explained Wu. “What sets us apart is that we continue our distinctive flavour profiles in wines with our unique varietals. They are not for everyone. But nine out of 10 people that drink Isabella or Niagara wines for the first time find it fresh – and they love it.”  Head winemaker Cai Jianlin, himself a local Yunnan farmer, ensures that vines are elevated from the ground to minimise spoilage. Harvest in July sees the farm swell to 200 people hand-harvesting the grapes. The estate, which includes tasting rooms and a restaurant, was one of the first in Yunnan open to wine tourism. “Our Niagara whites go well with Sichuan, Yunnan, Thai and Vietnamese cuisines – the sweetness on the nose and acidity on the palette cuts through spicy dishes,” said Wu. Also recommended is Cantonese roast meats (or siu mei) with Isabella reds, which are comparable to elegant Pinot Noirs. 

Premium red

In 2015, Yunnan Red launched its first premium red made entirely from hand-selecting the best Le Pourpre of the season. Named Dance in the Clouds and at 13.8% ABV, only half a dozen editions have been produced as the harvest that year must yield enough for a minimum of 2,000 bottles.  Dance in the Clouds is aged for 12 to 18 months in French or American oak barrels before a further 12 to 18 months in bottles; the 2023 edition is next to be launched. The 2018 edition currently retails at HK$900 (£85.25) as a starting price compared to the majority of Yunnan Red wines, which retails starting at HK$100 (£9.50). “Dance is more European-style, with notes of ripe blackberries and blueberries alongside fine and well-integrated tannins,” stated Wu. 

Adapting to the thirst for low-ABV

In response to evolving market trends, the most recent addition to Yunnan Red’s portfolio is its lower alcohol wine, available in cans as well as bottles. At 7% ABV with no added sugar, it is a sweeter alternative to the table wines.  The explosion in e-commerce has completely changed how Chinese consumers purchase Yunnan Red, with approximately half of all sales conducted online through popular platforms including Tmall, Red Book and WeChat. In tandem with KOL and influencer collaborations, one of the ways that Yunnan Red stands out in a crowded digital arena is its locally sourced art-driven labels.  “There are more than 30 ethnic minorities in Yunnan,” Wu said. “We want our heritage to stand front and centre. Our label art, which is purchased or commissioned, is very detailed, rich and colourful. They are very much about the place and help distinguish us.”

Looking ahead

Yunnan Red has historically concentrated on domestic distribution and expanded to Hong Kong in the late 2010s. Its on-trade partners include Rosewood Hong Kong, Regent Hong Kong and JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong.  “We are looking at possibly reaching out to Southeast Asian countries,” he said. “As the domestic market can absorb all of our products, we want to concentrate on regions that will benefit from our efforts if we were to expand.” Wu is proud that many Chinese people’s first experience with wine was sipping Yunnan Red: “There are plenty of producers, including importers, selling at price points of HK$500 (£47.30) and up. Our flavour profile of fruitiness with softer tannins was designed for entry level consumers. And our market is really everyday consumers who want easy drinking.”

title: Why Africa is the wine industry’s biggest missed opportunity
summary:
As traditional wine markets stagnate, producers continue to chase shrinking demand in Europe and North America. Benjamin Jack argues that the industry's greatest long-term opportunity lies in Africa – and those who delay risk arriving too late.

The post Why Africa is the wine industry’s biggest missed opportunity  appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
As traditional wine markets stagnate, producers continue to chase shrinking demand in Europe and North America. Benjamin Jack argues that the industry's greatest long-term opportunity lies in Africa – and those who delay risk arriving too late.

There is a particular quality to a good lunch in the European sunshine that makes the serious things feel manageable. After touring a Port lodge owned by a friend, somewhere between the starters and a second bottle of Vinho Verde, the discussion drifted, as it often does, to Africa. It happens more often than you might expect. Conversations that begin with wine inevitably end up on logistics, distribution margins and the buying habits of Lagos's emerging professional class. Africa has a habit of pulling the discussion back to itself for anyone thinking about where the drinks industry is heading rather than where it has been. Perhaps that is because I am from the continent. Or perhaps Europeans are simply looking in the wrong place.

Africa is the overlooked growth market

We all know the western wine market is under pressure. European consumption is declining and the American market, long the industry's great prize, is softening. The consumers the industry has spent decades cultivating are ageing, drinking less, and being told with increasing fervour by a wellness culture that whatever they are drinking is too much. The industry's response, broadly, has been to look inward, to “premiumise”, to produce alcohol-free alternatives, to chase the same shrinking pool of consumers with more sophisticated marketing. Few seem to be looking south. The African Development Bank estimates that over 350 million Africans now fall into a global-equivalent of middle class, a figure that is expanding faster than anywhere else in the world, concentrated in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, South Africa, and Côte d'Ivoire. That number is projected to surpass 500 million by 2030. Africa's urban population, 45% of the continent today, is forecast to double to 1.4 billion by 2050, making it home to one of the world's largest urban populations. Each year, urban Africa grows by an estimated 24 million people. Twenty-four million people, every year, moving into cities, many entering the consumer class, and developing the tastes and aspirations that go with urban professional life. Wine has arguably been a city drink since Roman times. In Africa wine follows urbanisation, disposable income, and aspiration the way water follows gravity. The conditions that created wine's rise in the developed world, a growing middle class with money to spend and a desire to signal their arrival in society, are now assembling themselves across an entire continent, at speed, and on a scale that dwarfs anything the European or American markets offered, even at their peak. The African wine market is forecast to reach 1.8 billion litres and $8 billion by 2035. And by any measure, that is a sizeable market. Now consider what the spirits and beer industries have already understood about all of this, because the contrast with wine is almost embarrassing.

Beer and spirits have already moved

Diageo got lucky in a sense. Their African brands have been present in Africa since the 1820s, when the first crates of Guinness arrived on the continent's shores. Today, with 86% local sourcing and manufacturing embedded across multiple African markets, their Africa strategy is not a future ambition, it is a present reality, built over two centuries of patient investment and route-to-market development. Their stated strategy on the continent is to grow their beer portfolio fast and their spirits brands faster. Heineken has recently moved with similar conviction. In South Africa in 2023, they formed Heineken Beverages, integrating Distell and Namibia Breweries into a single multi-category Southern African platform, covering beer, cider, RTDs, wine and spirits, with phased synergies executing through 2025 and further consolidation planned beyond. This is not exploratory. This is structural commitment. They have been asking the question: “Where are opportunities going to be in 20 years?”. That’s called strategic prescience. Both companies absorb demographic data for a living. Both companies looked at Africa's urbanisation curve, its population growth, its emerging middle class, its youthful consumer base, and made long-term bets accordingly. They did not wait for the market to come to them. They are building the infrastructure, the distribution, the brand presence, and the local relationships. Apart from a handful of producers ­– such as Gérard Bertrand, Rutini and Concha y Toro – the wine industry has largely watched from the sidelines.

The opportunity is already emerging

My father has spent his entire career trying to sell wine into Africa. This is more than a family anecdote. For most of those decades, the results were modest. The infrastructure was difficult, the distribution unreliable, the consumer base too small, the economics marginal. He persisted because he believed in the continent's trajectory, but the market was not yet ready to meet that belief halfway. In the last seven years, that has changed. Not just minimally, but materially. The same markets that resisted for decades have opened, and the change is not incidental. It tracks precisely with the economic development data: rising urban incomes, expanding middle class, improved logistics infrastructure, and something harder to quantify but impossible to ignore, a shift in how wine is perceived across the continent. Real cultural change in understanding what wine means in a vibrant, solution-led African culture. This is the point that the industry consistently underestimates. Wine in Africa is not just a drink. It is a status signal, an aspirational marker, a symbol of arrival into a certain kind of professional and social life. In other words, it mirrors the role wine has long played in Europe and North America. The IWSR has noted that Champagne and sparkling wine are highly sought after by aspirational, status-conscious African consumers, with meaningful opportunity in the affordable sparkling segment targeting the emerging middle class. The category is already carrying cultural weight on the continent. It simply lacks the industry infrastructure to meet the demand that weight is generating. This is not a market that needs to be convinced that wine matters, while Europe now is. Africa just needs the industry to show up.

The real risk is waiting too long

The question I hear most often when this conversation comes up is some version of: is it too early? And I understand the instinct, because the infrastructure challenges are real, the market complexity is genuine, the geopolitical and economic risks across 54 countries are daunting to the developed West. Like the USA and Europe, Africa is not a single market and anyone who treats it as one will learn that lesson quickly. But the question of whether it is too early is the wrong question. The right question is whether you think you are strong enough to wait and risk arriving late and negotiate from weakness, paying the premium that always accompanies belatedness, fighting for shelf space and consumer attention in markets where the beer and spirits categories have already spent decades building loyalty and distribution depth. Diageo and Heineken did not ask whether it was too early. They asked what position they needed to be in when the opportunity arrived, and then they built that position, over years and decades, at considerable cost and patience. The wine industry, watching their traditional western market contract, may be running out of time while continuing to invest in increasingly marginal solutions. There are, of course, genuine complexities. Wine faces specific challenges in Africa that spirits do not. It is more fragile in transit than beer, more sensitive to temperature than spirits, more dependent on cold chain infrastructure that is still developing across much of the continent. It is more expensive at entry level than the category alternatives like beer competing for the same disposable income. Religious and cultural factors vary significantly by country and region, in ways that require local knowledge rather than continental generalisations. None of these challenges are insurmountable. All of them are knowable. And all of them have been faced and solved, in adjacent categories, by companies willing to invest the time and capital to understand markets properly before dismissing them as too complicated. It just requires patient, relationship-led, locally-informed market development that does not expect immediate returns but understands that the long-term position being built is worth the investment required to build it. This is not a model that requires a multinational budget. It requires a long-term perspective, the discipline to hold it and most importantly, presence in the market – pack your dancing shoes and mozzie spray.

From export market to strategic priority

Ambitious wine businesses need an Africa strategy. Not a vague aspiration, not a few export containers sent speculatively into Johannesburg or Nairobi, but a coordinated, well-resourced, long-term commitment to building presence, distribution, and consumer relationships across the continent's key urban markets. They need the right partners and the right people on the ground. This means investing in local partnerships and importer relationships that understand route-to-market infrastructure. It means investing in consumer education that is culturally savvy and locally relevant, rather than transplanted from a patronising European perspective of African sophistication. It means accepting that the returns will not arrive on a quarterly reporting cycle and finding the capital structure to accommodate that reality. Africa is not China, the same rules don’t apply, neither do the boom and bust characteristics. It means, above all, taking seriously the possibility that the answer to the western wine market's structural decline is not to be found in another premiumisation strategy or another alcohol-free SKU, but in an entirely different part of the world, one that has been signalling its readiness for years to anyone paying attention. My father paid attention for decades. The market is finally proving him right. Africa is not the future of the wine market. It is the present.

Is the wine industry ‘missing the mark’ with new consumers?

title: Beer Hour: Mark Tranter
summary:
Burning Sky Brewery, based in the village of Firle at the base of the South Downs in East Sussex, was set up by Mark Tranter in 2013. Jessica Mason finds out more about the man behind the beers and how each of his confident brews gains both a mix of unbridled interest from beer fans with an enviable reputation for quality.

The post Beer Hour: Mark Tranter appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Burning Sky Brewery, based in the village of Firle at the base of the South Downs in East Sussex, was set up by Mark Tranter in 2013. Jessica Mason finds out more about the man behind the beers and how each of his confident brews gains both a mix of unbridled interest from beer fans with an enviable reputation for quality. “Like most things in life, my role has evolved,” Tranter explains, describing how far Burning Sky has come since its early days. In the beginning, Tranter says he was “the only full timer”. But nowadays, whilst he is “still keenly involved in production and recipe development” rather a lot of what he does involves “planning and reacting to and with the changing marketplace” - keeping the brewery relevant, although, “without losing the essence of what Burning Sky means to me and others”. This is no mean feat, because breweries as successful as Burning Sky are often shaped by their climb into something that can often morph the blueprint of initial intentions. But not Burning Sky. There is an adamance for independent integrity and vision that shows an admirable strength of character and conviction. Prior to Burning Sky, Tranter was with Dark Star from 1996 to 2013 and saw that brewery grow from a tiny pub brewery to a relatively large production brewery. “There are too many experiences to write about, but working with great people and making something tangible is what matters to me at the end of the day,” he says. That meaningfulness has never been lost along the way. Nor is there a shred of complacency. You get the sense that Tranter’s loyalty towards those who have helped him along the way - especially when there was nothing for them to gain - will continue forevermore. But also that he has never overlooked how tiny, sometimes seemingly insignificant acts have shaped him, assisted his journey and fine-tuned his approach. Some might say that 'timing is everything'. Sometimes, it works in our favour. Other times, the universe has other ideas.

The butterfly effect

“I don't necessarily believe in fate but it is strange how your life is changed by being somewhere at a certain time due to something else that happened earlier that day, or a few days, weeks, or months previously,” he says and explains: “My career in brewing would not have existed if I wasn't in the Evening Star pub and, somewhat randomly, offered a job by (the late) Rob Jones.” When describing Jones, this is where Tranter really taps into showing how an unspoken level of understanding and intuition between them played a vital role. Jones changed his life. He was perceptive and, as Tranter describes: “His maverick approach suited me and together we created some great beers. That esoteric creativity is what makes Burning Sky.” Tranter is quite at home in pubs. Quietly standing beer-in-hand, his favourite watering holes are the kinds of establishments where the beer is fresh and the people who run the place are as genuine and as welcoming as their decor. Everyone welcomes him with a smile, his face is known, he often drinks in the same venues too. Meeting Tranter in a pub is also, probably, the best way to really assess his palate. When relaxed, he’ll opt for what’s on cask and look at the line-up for its seasonal appeal. As such, his beer order “really depends on the time of year”. But, he admits, “a great cask beer, in tip top condition and served cool, is pretty hard to beat”.

Appreciation for others

What’s he drinking? “I generally lean towards pale ales, on cask or keg, but love well-executed mixed fermentation beers including of course the great Gueuzes of Pajottenland. I'm also known to enjoy lagers, stouts and porters” he adds. His repertoire is broad and yet the way he embraces so many beer styles makes his interest in beer playfully relatable in its unfixed variety. He shows appreciation for everything having its place and reason for existing. You've got to love that. If there were any philosophical guidance out there in the world that has ever resonated with Tranter then it would be “treat others as you would wish to be treated” says Tranter, pointing out that it can often help to “remember the title of the book by Seth Tobocman You don't have to f*ck people over to survive”. Despite this, lately, survival has been an ever-present goal for many breweries across the country. Tranter looks back at what has been a changeable beer landscape in Britain and considers how things have shifted and rarely stood still. He explains: “The sector is constantly evolving and having been involved in it for longer than seems real, there has been more changes, both positive and negative, than I would have ever imagined. Since 2020, the marketplace has been in a constant state of flux but for all the doom and gloom, it seems to me to be stabilising.”

Tackling the issues

With this in mind, Tranter says that “survival and being able to adapt [and] react is what's needed” for most brewers. But what are the real challenges of the day affecting the sector? There are, indeed, so many. And yet, despite being thwarted by challenges, the beer industry still manages to muster some verve, do what is necessary to stay in the game and continually reassess its relevance. “There are so many issues at the moment from increased costs directly to us, pub closures and people not drinking [or] going out as much,” Tranter observes, but adds: “If I stopped to think about it all too much, I probably wouldn't get out of bed in the morning.” But in the case of not being able to wield any control over what happens within the sector, Tranter also makes a shrewd point in stating that there are things that fall within his remit - he can put something into the world that he knows is truly good. He can create. And can be an artist in a world of rules and roadblocks. He can, figuratively and literally, take to the hills and do what he wants. And he does.

Astute and perceptive

He says: “As a small producer, there is little we can do other than give our customers the best quality, value and service that we can - all of those things have been essential to Burning Sky since our inception. And we are still here.” In many ways the staying power that Burning Sky has demonstrated is not accidental. Instead, it is due to the way that Tranter and his team has remained engaged. As such, the business has stayed astute and perceptive. Tranter explains: “If you engage in the industry that you are part of, on every level your products will naturally remain relevant. By this I mean, if you engage as both producer and consumer, you will be aware of the shifting sands and how your products can move with them, without disappearing or losing their essence.” But then, he adds: “It doesn't get any easier” but also highlights “nor does it get less enjoyable and just when you think you've reached the top, there is another peak to climb”. Are there parts of the inner-workings of the beer industry that really aren’t ideal? “That disposable culture has infiltrated everything, including beer and a lot of people are more bothered about something new than something great,” he says. But, never one to not offer both sides of the coin, Tranter is quick to assess the positives and says that “on the flip-side, it's great to see traditional pubs being embraced and many of them in turn offering a greater selection of independently-produced drinks than ever before”. Finding ways to retain a balanced view and always look at things with fresh eyes helps to recalibrate and see the bigger picture, he says. This, he finds on the South Downs and, indeed, anywhere around the world where the open space and countryside beckons.

Funny, considerate, sensitive, humble, confident

“As for me, individually, just getting out on the hills keeps me sane. Whether it is walking to work, a long walk at the weekend, or a multi-day place-to-place hike, these make me want to get out of the door as soon as possible,” he says, explaining: “I am fortunate that my partner shares this love and it is something that we experience together”. In terms of future plans and aspirations, Tranter places his trust in those he works among. He explains that one day, “hopefully, the brewery will continue to thrive in its own little way and the wonderful group of people that work there will take control and boot me out of the door and onto the hills”. This perspective also perfectly echoes his belief that “to do what is best for those around you, will generally have a positive effect on yourself”. Ask Simon Gane, who does all of the artwork for Burning Sky, how he would describe Tranter - who he has known since he was about 15 years old - and you learn more about his rarer traits. Not just because, by Gane’s own admission Tranter is “funny as f*ck”. But also because his humour gives way to more scarce qualities and you discover someone “considerate, sensitive and humble, but deceptively confident too”. It is this confidence that shines through in his brews. After all, Tranter is someone who has the courage of his convictions and this will come in handy “if you’re ageing a sh*tload of beer”.

title: ‘People are drinking differently today,’ says Australian Vintage CMO
summary:
Small format wines are nothing new. But thanks to an "innovative" approach and bold branding, Poco Vino is satisfying a market segment whose needs "have never been stronger", explains Emily Harper, chief marketing officer at Australian Vintage.

The post ‘People are drinking differently today,’ says Australian Vintage CMO appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Small format wines are nothing new. But thanks to an "innovative" approach and bold branding, Poco Vino is satisfying a market segment whose needs "have never been stronger", explains Emily Harper, chief marketing officer at Australian Vintage. With a colour-forward marketing campaign, plus a wholehearted embrace of the term ‘Sauvy B’ and the phrase ‘less faff, more fun’, it is fair to say that Poco Vino is fluent in vibes. The Australian Vintage brand launched last year – winning a Drinks Business Award in the process – and immediately leaned into informal stylings and social media-ready moments. These are, after all, the native languages of its Zillennial target market. Style and substance, however, are not mutually exclusive. Its foundations are recognisable – the single serve and pre-eminent grape varieties. Yet, in packaging them for the modern drinker, Poco Vino is addressing very real consumer concerns. “Yes, small format already exists in wine, but it’s in its infancy and hasn’t been done in an innovative way,” explains Emily Harper, chief marketing officer at Australian Vintage. “Whilst the size isn’t new, the consumer needs it is addressing have never been stronger. People are drinking differently today – they’re looking for convenience, moderation and quality. Poco Vino delivers a wine experience in a format that is stylish, sleek and suits modern lifestyles.” Before launching, Australian Vintage ran research panels with more than 3,000 consumers in seven markets. What the team found was a range of barriers to wine when choosing a 75cl bottle: it limits exploration, it ties several drinkers to one style, and it makes it difficult to moderate intake. Poco Vino therefore borrows from success elsewhere in FMCG retail – it makes a wine snackable. The bottles are small, light and even stack, making them easy to transport and to store. That lends itself to drinking at home, but equally applies to picnics or events.

Grabbing attention – and keeping it simple

With bold colours each pertaining to a variety or style – Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay, rosé, Pinot Noir, Malbec and Shiraz – the range is immediately accessible. Even if consumers are increasingly adventurous in their drinking, it is still recognisable varieties in classic expressions that drive attention – “a simple, trusted way for many consumers to choose a wine”, as Harper summarises. Indeed, in a sometimes opaque industry, the aim has been to reduce any feeling of overwhelm in the consumer. “Today’s shoppers are making decisions in increasingly busy retail environments, so a brand needs to capture attention quickly,” Harper says. “Poco Vino’s distinctive branding and strong shelf merchandising help the range stand out and make it easy for consumers to discover the product.” Still, any brand can only succeed if it retains customers. The focus on quality wine that drinkers want to return to is just as strong as in other Australian Vintage brands. Poco Vino now sells roughly 12,000 bottles a day around the world, earning a firm following. A strong brand is only the beginning,” Harper says. “The quality of the wine is what builds trust, drives repeat purchase and encourages consumers to explore the category further. The branding and merchandising make wine more accessible, while the wine itself delivers the experience that keeps consumers coming back.”
